first.rationale: Both live symptoms (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) sit on the same funnel, and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly addresses both with one slot. memory_86 and memory_31 both point at onboarding/signup friction as a durable lever, and memory_91 supports activation messaging as the alternative — so the two verifications I want are memory_86 (most recent and directly on the declining metric) and memory_91 (the strongest competing use of the slot). I am deliberately NOT choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records acquisition/revenue lift but a material 30-day retention drop and an explicit instruction not to generalize it, and the objective here is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not short-term acquisition. That is the main downstream value risk — chasing the competitor on price would buy churn-prone logos and degrade the very metric we are optimizing. Secondary risk: onboarding simplification can inflate completion and activation counts while lowering downstream account quality (memory_31's lift was measured at first-week activation, not at revenue), so the experiment must carry retention and qualified-revenue guardrails rather than declaring victory on funnel metrics. Uncertainty preserved: the inherited memories are pre-competitor-entry and may not describe today's mix of price-sensitive SMB traffic; if the archive shows memory_86's lift came from a segment unlike our current inbound, or that its effect was measured only on completion rather than downstream value, I would shift the slot to activation_messaging (memory_91) as the cheaper in-product intervention. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) and referral_incentive (memory_57) are both credible but neither targets the two metrics that actually moved this quarter.

final.rationale: Verification strengthened the onboarding case rather than undercutting it: exp_86 shows completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and — critically — 30-day retention +3%, so the lift was not a funnel-inflation artifact but carried downstream value. exp_91 is also genuinely confirmed (engagement +11%, activation +6%, retention +1%), so activation_messaging is a real fallback rather than a bad option. I choose simplify_onboarding because onboarding sits upstream of activation, so it plausibly addresses both declining metrics (-4% completion, -6% activation) with the single slot, and its verified retention effect (+3%) is the larger of the two on the dimension the objective actually cares about: sustainable long-term qualified revenue. I continue to reject promotional_pricing despite the competitor's aggressive entry pricing. memory_73 remains the sharpest constraint in memory: real acquisition and revenue lift, but a material 30-day retention drop and an explicit instruction not to generalize it. Matching a price attack would buy churn-prone, price-shopping logos and degrade the exact metric being optimized — that is the primary downstream value risk here, and answering a pricing threat with a retention/time-to-value improvement is the more durable response. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving away: both source records predate the competitor's entry, so today's inbound mix is likely more price-sensitive than the population those experiments ran on, and the historical effect sizes may not transfer at full magnitude. A shortened flow can also admit lower-intent accounts, so I hold this at a standard experiment with proper controls rather than a broad rollout, and I instrument 30-day retention and qualified revenue per cohort — not just completion and activation counts — as the decision criteria. If retention regresses against control even while completion rises, that falsifies the transfer assumption and the slot shifts to activation_messaging next cycle.
